title: The picture we do not discuss
paras: The picture we don't discuss — that's where I want to start. But first: if you or a colleague are struggling, help is there right now. You don't have to hit a threshold before you reach for it — earlier is better than later. The Samaritans are free, day or night, on one one six, one two three. Shout is a twenty-four-seven crisis text line — text eight five two five eight. And if you're in immediate danger, call nine nine nine. There's a fuller directory near the end, in 'Where to turn'.

Here's the argument. Mental health at work is a leadership and management issue long before it's a wellbeing perk. A caseload no one can carry, or a committee that abuses the officer in front of it — you don't fix those with a meditation app. What helps is workload control, senior colleagues who model and notice, and a structured programme of support.

And planning is a caring profession that isn't much good at caring for its own. The wider built environment is one of the worst sectors in the country for mental ill health — the suicide rate among construction workers runs at around three point seven times the national average, and there's talk of a silent crisis of suicide across it. A 2025 survey found eighty per cent of construction workers had felt stressed over the previous year, sixty-eight per cent anxiety, and thirty-eight per cent depression. The planning figures are thinner, but the conditions are familiar — heavy caseloads, deadlines that never stop, chronic under-resourcing, and a culture that mistakes stoicism for competence.

Put that against the national picture. The 2017 Thriving at Work review found around one in seven people at work have symptoms of a mental health condition, some three hundred thousand with long-term conditions lose their jobs every year, and poor mental health costs employers between thirty-three and forty-two billion pounds a year. So this isn't a soft, optional concern. It's a workforce problem, a retention problem, and — for public bodies already short of planners — a capacity problem. Treating wellbeing as a perk rather than as core to running a service is part of why the service is short-staffed.

One word on how this guide works. The detailed sourcing — who found what, and how firm each figure is — lives in the written guide, so I'll keep us on the ideas. Where the piece takes a position it's flagged as a PlanRef view, my own opinion, and I'll say so. And please be aware: this piece discusses work-related distress and suicide.

title: The public-facing injury
paras: Now, the public-facing injury — because planners carry a stressor desk-bound professions don't. Planning is where the public most often collides with the state over what they care about most: their home, their street, their view. And the officer is the face of that decision. In a small but real proportion of cases it turns into hostility — planners followed while driving, vehicles vandalised, abused on social media, treated badly by elected members at committee. It's part of a wider surge in abuse of people in public life, which the Local Government Association has taken on through 'Debate Not Hate', and which the R-T-P-I is now tackling through a Safety of Planners working group and a partnership with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust on personal safety.

And even short of abuse, the everyday job carries what psychologists call emotional labour — staying calm and professional while you absorb other people's anger, disappointment and fear. Add the moral weight of recommending refusal, taking enforcement action, or defending an unpopular allocation without controlling the outcome — in public, by name, at a microphone. A single hostile committee, or one confrontational site visit, can sit with an officer for days. The instinct is to treat it as part of the job and say nothing — and that's precisely the instinct that lets it build up unseen.

title: What Covid and home working changed
paras: So — what did Covid and home working change? It rewired how planners work, and the settlement is double-edged. For most people, hybrid and home working are a real gain: flexibility, no commute, time back for family and exercise, and better access to the profession for carers and disabled planners. Surveys keep finding the majority want to keep at least some remote working and describe it positively. Any honest treatment starts there — a nostalgic 'back to the office' reflex misreads what people value.

But the same shift carries a quieter cost, unevenly spread, and isolation is the core of it. One study of over half a million workers put roughly a third of the rise in mental distress since the pandemic down to remote work — remote workers spending an extra hour a day alone, and those living alone hit hardest. The boundary between work and home erodes: the commute that marked the end of the day is gone, the laptop's always on the kitchen table, and 'always on' becomes the norm. And the informal repairs of an office go with it — the overheard 'you all right?', the corridor debrief after a bruising meeting, the colleague who notices you've gone quiet. Those happened by accident; in a hybrid world you have to make them happen on purpose.

And it hits hardest the group the profession most needs to keep: early-career planners. Recent research found nearly half of eighteen-to-twenty-four-year-olds say hybrid working makes workplace relationships harder; over four in ten fear it restricts their development; more than a quarter feel disconnected, rising to thirty-six per cent of entry-level staff; and only sixteen per cent of entry-level employees get regular feedback. A graduate who joined remotely may never pick up the tacit craft that used to pass across a desk — handling a difficult objector, how a committee report is really written, when to worry about a case — and may have no one who'd notice they're drowning. What they wanted wasn't table football, it was structure: check-ins, mental health support, clear career paths, in-person mentoring.

Now a PlanRef view — my own opinion, on hybrid working. The answer to isolation isn't to march everyone back five days a week; that throws away a real gain and costs you good people, carers especially and the early-career staff you're trying to keep. The answer is to do deliberately what the office did by accident. If connection, mentoring and noticing no longer happen on their own, design them in: check-ins in the calendar, mentoring that's assigned rather than hoped for, and enough in-person time for the human contact that catches problems early. The office was never magic — it was a machine for accidental support, now switched off unless you rebuild it on purpose.

title: The value of senior colleagues
paras: Let me turn to senior colleagues — the single most effective, least expensive intervention in workplace mental health. Not a policy, not an app: a more experienced person who manages or mentors a team and does a few unglamorous things well. Their influence is out of all proportion, because the line-manager relationship is the biggest day-to-day determinant of how someone experiences work. It sorts into three duties.

First: manage the workload. It's the biggest lever, and it dwarfs everything else — no amount of resilience training, counselling or mindfulness offsets a caseload too big to carry, and pretending otherwise tells staff the problem is their weakness rather than the volume. The recognised stress framework puts 'demands' at the top of six things an employer has to manage — demands, control, support, relationships, role and change. A good senior colleague protects the team from unrealistic demand rather than passing it through: prioritising ruthlessly and saying so, pushing back upward when the work exceeds the resource, making it acceptable to hand a case back, and treating a permanently overloaded planner as a management failure to fix, not a performance to criticise. The determination clock and the political pressure won't vanish — but how they land on an individual is a choice the manager makes.

Second: model it, notice it, and signpost — don't try to fix it. Culture is set from the top by behaviour, not statements. A head of service who answers emails at eleven at night, never takes lunch and never takes leave teaches the team that's the standard; one who takes their holiday, guards their evenings and talks openly about their own hard periods gives everyone permission to be human. Beyond that, notice — hold regular, unhurried one-to-ones and ask twice, 'no, how are you really?', watching for the changes before a crisis: withdrawal, cynicism, uncharacteristic mistakes, a good planner going quiet. And when someone discloses, your role is not to be the therapist. It's to listen without diagnosing, know the routes — the employee assistance programme, occupational health, the R-T-P-I helpline, the G-P, the Samaritans — and walk them to the door of the right help while adjusting the work so recovery is possible.

Third: back your people against abuse. Senior colleagues have a non-negotiable duty to stand behind their officers — public support for one attacked at committee or by an applicant, not a diplomatic silence; robust policies on abuse and lone-worker safety that are actually used; and a debrief and check-in after the hostile meeting or difficult site visit, rather than moving straight to the next case. An officer who knows the organisation will back them can absorb a great deal. One who feels exposed and alone can't — and will eventually leave.

title: A programme of support
paras: That brings us to a programme of support. Good individual managers are necessary but not sufficient — they come and go, and their quality varies. What turns good intentions into something dependable is a programme: a structured, named, resourced set of support that doesn't rely on having a kind boss. The evidence and the survey responses agree — people want structure, not gestures.

Start with mentoring and peer support. Mentoring is the backbone, and its wellbeing value is underestimated because it's misunderstood — a mentor isn't a counsellor and shouldn't try to be. The value is prevention, early detection and connection: a trusted person outside the line-management chain, somewhere to say 'I'm struggling' without it being a performance issue, someone honest about their own hard spells who dismantles the belief that everyone else is coping, and often first to spot the early signs. The infrastructure exists — the R-T-P-I runs a mentoring scheme, and many firms and authorities run buddying for new entrants. It costs little to give that a wellbeing dimension and make it assigned rather than optional, so the quiet junior who'd never seek a mentor gets given one. Peer-support networks and structured buddying, for returners and anyone carrying contentious casework, do the same laterally.

Then mindfulness and the individual tools — useful, and not a substitute. The trials show mindfulness-based programmes give small-to-moderate reductions in stress for individuals, and apps help at the margin, so for someone who finds it useful it's a legitimate tool. The caveat: it addresses the individual's response to pressure, not the pressure itself. And there's a well-aimed critique — 'McMindfulness' — that employers reach for it because it's cheaper and less confronting than fixing workload, and that offering meditation to a team drowning in cases reads as telling them their stress is a personal failing to breathe away. So the honest position is simple: individual coping tools — mindfulness, exercise, sleep, boundaries, talking therapies — are worth having and offering, but they sit on top of the structural fixes, never instead of them. Mindfulness with a lighter caseload is support; the same session instead of one is a fig leaf.

So what does a good programme look like? A clear, communicated plan that names the support. Line managers trained to hold a wellbeing conversation — most are promoted for technical skill and never taught this. A confidential route to real help through an employee assistance programme and occupational health. Mental Health First Aiders to spot signs and signpost — useful, though training them raises awareness more than it changes outcomes, so they supplement good management rather than replace it. Assigned mentoring and peer support. And underneath it all, honest monitoring of workload and wellbeing, so the organisation notices trouble before it becomes turnover. None of this is exotic — and most of it is cheap, set against the cost of losing and replacing experienced planners.

title: The duties behind all of this
paras: A word on the duties behind all of this — because if you need the argument in the language of obligation rather than decency, they're real. Employers owe a duty of care, and health-and-safety law extends to work-related stress, which they're expected to assess and manage, using that same framework of demands, control, support, relationships, role and change. And under the Equality Act, a mental health condition can amount to a disability, and where it does the employer must make reasonable adjustments and must not discriminate.

Beyond that, the Thriving at Work standards set out what good looks like — a mental-health plan, awareness, open conversations, decent working conditions, effective people management and routine monitoring. There's now a global standard, published in 2021, for managing psychological health and safety at work, and many public bodies have signed the Mental Health at Work Commitment. The direction is the same: psychological safety is moving from a nice-to-have to a managed obligation — and the organisations ahead of that curve are the ones that'll keep their people.

title: What it comes down to
paras: So what does it come down to? For the individual planner, a few things genuinely help, without waiting for permission: talk to someone early rather than at crisis, use support before you're desperate, protect your boundaries even when the caseload resists, debrief the bad days, and treat asking for help as a professional skill, not a failure. But the weight of this piece sits on the organisation and the senior colleague, because that's where the leverage is: an individual can manage their response to an impossible job, but only the organisation can make the job possible.

The thread through all of it is that wellbeing is built, not bolted on — in the size of the caseload, the behaviour of the person at the top, the mentor a graduate is actually given, the debrief after the hostile committee, the programme that doesn't depend on luck. Get those right and the app and the fruit basket are pleasant extras; get them wrong and no perk will hold the profession together. The planners we lose to burnout and abuse aren't weak — very often they're the ones who cared the most, in a system that didn't care enough for them. That's a choice, and it can be made differently.

One last PlanRef view — my opinion, and the verdict. If you run a team: the most powerful mental-health intervention you control isn't a meditation-app subscription. It's a manageable caseload, your own visible example, and a mentor for every junior who needs one. Reach for mindfulness and resilience training first and you're treating the symptom while leaving the cause — worse, telling an overloaded, abused workforce their distress is a personal shortcoming to breathe away. Fix the workload, back your officers in public, build support into the structure rather than pinning it to the kitchen wall — and the softer tools finally do some good on top. Wellbeing is a leadership responsibility, and delegating it to an app is the tell of an organisation that's decided not to lead.

title: Where to turn
paras: Where to turn. If you or a colleague are struggling, these are the main routes — and there's no threshold you have to reach first. Earlier is better than later.

In a crisis, or if you just need to talk: the Samaritans are free, day or night, on one one six, one two three — or by email, at jo at samaritans dot org. Shout is a free, twenty-four-seven crisis text line — text eight five two five eight. And if life is in immediate danger, call nine nine nine.

For planners: the R-T-P-I offers members a free mental health and wellbeing helpline and a wellbeing hub, plus free legal advice, through the R-T-P-I website — along with its emerging Safety of Planners guidance on abuse and lone-worker safety.

Across the built environment: LionHeart supports R-I-C-S professionals and their families, with counselling and practical help. And Mates in Mind, and the Lighthouse Construction Industry Charity — which runs a twenty-four-seven helpline — support the wider construction sector.

And through work and the N-H-S: there's your employer's Employee Assistance Programme — confidential counselling, usually free — and occupational health. There are N-H-S Talking Therapies, with self-referral in England for anxiety and depression. And there's your G-P. Mind's Mental Health at Work portal, and the Hub of Hope directory, will help you find more.

title: Practice points
paras: Finally, the practice points, mostly for senior colleagues and organisations. One: wellbeing is capacity, not perk — poor mental health costs employers between thirty-three and forty-two billion pounds a year. Two: workload is the biggest lever — no app offsets an unmanageable caseload, so protect the team and push back upward. Three: name the public-facing injury — abuse, emotional labour and moral weight are real occupational stressors. Four: back your officers in public, and debrief after hostile meetings. Five: model it from the top — take your leave and talk openly about pressure.

Six: notice, and ask twice — watch for withdrawal, cynicism, a good planner going quiet. Seven: signpost, don't diagnose — know the routes and walk people to them. Eight: do on purpose what the office did by accident — build connection and mentoring into hybrid working. Nine: protect the early-career hardest — thirty-six per cent of entry-level staff feel disconnected, only sixteen per cent get regular feedback; they want check-ins and in-person mentoring. Ten: assign mentors — the quiet junior who'd never ask most needs one.

Eleven: mindfulness on top, never instead. Twelve: build a programme, not a poster — a plan, trained managers, a confidential route through the employee assistance programme and occupational health, first aiders, assigned mentoring, and honest monitoring. Thirteen: know the duties — the duty of care and stress standards, the Equality Act's reasonable adjustments, Thriving at Work and the global psychological-safety standard. Fourteen: ask for help early — a skill, not a failure. And fifteen: the ones we lose often cared the most — burnout and abuse take the committed, not the weak.

title: Sources
paras: And to close — the sources. Rather than read a bibliography aloud, the full source list is in the written guide: every figure here is attributed there, with its date and how firm it is. One caveat — survey and prevalence figures get restated over time, so re-check the headline statistics against the primary source before you rely on them. This was written for England and the U-K, and the support links change too, so check those before leaning on them.
And if you're struggling — the Samaritans are free on one one six, one two three, day or night.
